Abstract
Object detection algorithm in urban trafﬁc using remote sensing images often suffers from high complexity, low real-time
performance, and low accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose RTL-Net, an urban trafﬁc object detection network
structure based on You Only Look Once (YOLO) v8s. To enhance real-time performance beyond the benchmark, we imple-
mented lightweight designs for the loss function, backbone, neck, and head components. Firstly, a Powerable-IoU (PIoU) loss
function was introduced to make the algorithm more suitable for different scales of targets and reduce false detection. Sec-
ondly, the Lightweight Shared Convolutional Detection (LSCD) head was replaced to ensure the detection performance and
signiﬁcantly improve the lightweight performance of the algorithm. Additionally, this paper introduces the Dilatation-wise
Residual (DWR) module to facilitate the algorithm’s extraction of detailed features. In addition, we optimize the Bidirec-
tional Feature Pyramid Network (Bi-FPN), enabling the fusion of multiple features to improve overall feature integration and
performance. The VisDrone2021 dataset was utilized for experimental training. Experimental results demonstrate that the
proposed algorithm achieves a signiﬁcant 43.9% reduction in parameters and an 18.9% decrease in computational complexity.
Moreover, the detection accuracy has improved by 2.3%, while maintaining a real-time detection speed of 263.2 frames per
second. For edge computing object detection, our method outperforms YOLOv8s and leading remote sensing algorithms in
both speed and accuracy, achieving state-of-the-art performance among single-stage detectors with comparable parameters.
Keywords Remote sensing · Feature fusion · Lightweight · Real-time detection

Introduction
THE rapid urbanization and transportation development have
led to increasingly complex road conditions with diverse and
dense trafﬁc participants, resulting in trafﬁc congestion and
heighteningsafetyconcerns.Consequently,accurateandefﬁ-
cient detection of targets in dense remote sensing images has
become increasingly signiﬁcant in intelligent transportation
systems for trafﬁc monitoring, autonomous driving, parking,
and other applications. Advances in remote sensing technol-
ogy enable the acquisition of large-scale scene images [1, 2].
Accurately detecting dense small targets from these complex
remote sensing images remains a signiﬁcant challenge [3–5].
Object detection algorithms for remote sensing images
have evolved through two main phases: traditional object
detection algorithms and deep learning-based object detec-
tion algorithms. Traditional algorithms relied on man-
ual feature extraction and pattern matching, using tech-
niques like edge detection, texture analysis, shape matching,
and template-based algorithms [6, 7]. Nevertheless, these
approaches are limited by several constraints, including low

detection accuracy, slow processing speed, high computa-
tional cost, and inadequate adaptability to dense scenes,
particularly when detecting dense small targets in com-
plex environments. In contrast, recent advancements in deep
learning have signiﬁcantly enhanced object detection in
remote sensing images. Algorithms such as YOLO [8], Faster
R-CNN [9, 10], and Single Shot Multi Box Detector (SSD)
[11] have demonstrated superior performance, offering high
precision, real-time capability, and robustness in complex
scenarios. However, these methods often struggle with the
unique challenges posed by remote sensing imagery, such
as dense object distributions and signiﬁcant scale varia-
tions. While recent object detection algorithms have achieved
improved accuracy through more complex and deep net-
works using convolutional neural networks [12], the pursuit
of greater accuracy often leads to increasingly complex and
resource-intensive models, making it difﬁcult to deploy these
solutions on mobile or edge devices.
Moreover, detecting objects in remote sensing images
is complicated by several real-world factors, including
small targets, high speed movement, complex scenes, lim-
ited extractable features, and signiﬁcant scale variations
[13], posing signiﬁcant challenges for existing detection
algorithms. To address these challenges while maintaining
computational efﬁciency, weproposeRTL-Net, alightweight
and efﬁcient object detection algorithm based on YOLOv8s,
speciﬁcally designed for real-time detection in remote sens-
ing imagery. Our contributions are as follows:
1) We introduce Powerful-IoU (PIoU), featuring an adap-
tive penalty factor and a gradient adjustment function
that dynamically adapts to varying object characteris-
tics, improving the accuracy of overlap measurements
and making the model more adaptable and stable across
varying object sizes, shapes, and poses.
2) We develop a lightweight shared convolutional detec-
tion (LSCD) head, which reduces both the model’s size
and computational cost without compromising detec-
tion performance. Through innovative parameter sharing
mechanisms, RTL-Net enhances detection speed and
suitability for resource-constrained devices.
3) We enhance the feature fusion network using a Bidi-
rectional Feature Pyramid Network (Bi-FPN), optimized
for multi-scale feature representation, improving target
recognition and localization in remote sensing images,
particularly under small, blurry, and complex conditions
while facilitating better transfer of high-level semantic
informationtolowerlayers,enhancingsmalltargetdetec-
tion.

Section “Related work” reviews related research on object

Related work
In the realm of remote sensing image detection, the grow-
ing demand for precise trafﬁc monitoring has led to a
predominant reliance on deep learning techniques [1–5].
Recent advances in feature extraction and multi-scale pro-
cessing have signiﬁcantly enhanced detection capabilities,
particularly for small objects and complex scenes [14, 15].
Deep learning-based object detection algorithms are primar-
ily categorized into two distinct approaches: two-stage and
single-stage methods.
Two-stage algorithms, such as R-CNN [6], ﬁrst generate
candidate boxes, then classify and reﬁne these proposals.
While these methods achieve high accuracy, they often suf-
fer from slower detection speeds and higher computational
requirements. The substantial computational overhead of
these models, particularly in terms of parameter count and
inference speed, makes them impractical for deployment on
edge computing devices such as UAVs, necessitating the
development of more lightweight alternatives [16].
In contrast, single-stage detection algorithms, typically
represented by YOLO (You Only Look Once) [8], aim to
streamline the detection process. YOLO directly convolves
and pools images to simultaneously generate candidate
frames, classify objects, and regress bounding boxes. This
uniﬁed approach achieves an optimal balance between detec-
tion speed and accuracy, making it especially advantageous
for real-time remote sensing applications where computa-
tional efﬁciency is crucial [15].
The single-stage YOLO algorithm has gained widespread
adoption in remote sensing image detection due to its abil-
ity to maintain a favorable trade-off between speed and
accuracy [17, 18], effectively meeting the demands of efﬁ-
cient and precise trafﬁc monitoring in urban environments.
Recent improvements in feature map processing and multi-
scale detection have further enhanced YOLO’s capabilities
for small object detection, particularly in complex urban
scenes. Consequently, achieving an optimal balance between
accuracy and computational efﬁciency remains a signiﬁcant
challenge in urban trafﬁc object detection [15]. Challenges
can be summarized into the following three points:
1) Detection accuracy in complex urban scenes with dense
backgrounds and diverse target characteristics requires
signiﬁcant enhancement.

2) The computational demands of complex network archi-

3) The simultaneous achievement of high precision and

To enhance the ability to extract structural information
from features, Li [19] et al. proposed an end-to-end method
that combines a target-guided feature super-resolution net-
work with a powerful feature fusion module to improve the
detection of small targets in remote sensing images. This
approach aligns with recent advances in feature extraction
techniques, demonstrating the importance of effective fea-
ture representation in small target detection. Meanwhile,
Gao [20] et al. developed a remote sensing image detec-
tion model based on fully convolutional one-stage object
detection, enhancing the positive sample sampling effect for
small or weak targets and signiﬁcantly improving the aver-
age detection accuracy of ﬁve types of vehicle targets in
remote sensing images. However, despite the enhancements
in accuracy, these improvements came at the cost of increased
computational complexity due to additional multi-feature
fusion operations, compromising the model’s efﬁciency.
Subsequently, Guo [21] et al. proposed an improved
vehicle detection algorithm based on YOLOv3, incorpo-
rating an adaptive fusion module to the feature extraction
network. The feature fusion network was also enhanced
with the cross-scale channel attention mechanism, and a
subpixel convolution module was introduced to detect and
extract vehicles’ explicit semantic information. Although the
improved algorithm signiﬁcantly enhanced vehicle detec-
tion accuracy, it exhibited a high miss rate for targets with
shadowed occlusions and dark backgrounds. Moreover, the
introduction of numerous parameters hindered deployment
on common embedded devices and adversely affected the
algorithm’s real-time performance.
To address the high miss rate problem, Ma [22] et al.
optimized the YOLOv5 algorithm for small and dense target
detection. Building upon recent advances in receptive-ﬁeld
attention and multi-scale feature processing [14], they recon-
structed the feature extraction network to enhance feature
diversity, reduce the computational burden, and effectively
extract potential remote sensing image features. To mitigate
interference from complex background noise, efﬁcient fea-
ture fusion blocks were integrated into the feature fusion
network. Finally, an efﬁcient decoupled head was added to
the network’s output, strengthening the model’s localization
and regression capabilities. However, although the optimized
algorithm showed speciﬁc improvements in target detection
performance, it still compromised the algorithm’s real-time
and lightweight performance.
A real-time object detection algorithm based on edge
computing was proposed by Cheng [23] et al. by introduc-
ing lightweight networks MobileNetV3, Multiscale-PANet
and Soft-Merge, improving upon the YOLOv4 algorithm.
While this approach achieved real-time performance through
architectural optimization, it failed to demonstrate signiﬁcant
improvements in detection accuracy, highlighting the ongo-
ing challenge of balancing speed and precision. Zhang [24] et
al., based on YOLOv5, integrated the triple attention mech-
anism into its backbone and designed a feature extraction
network structure for small target objects to retain important
feature information better. Additionally, they designed two
types of pyramid pooling structures in the feature fusion net-
work to enhance feature fusion at different scales and enrich
target feature information. The improved network increased
the average accuracy of target detection by 1.7%.
To sum up, while the above research has signiﬁcantly
advanced object detection algorithms for remote sensing
images from various individual considerations, achieving an
optimal balance between accuracy and computational efﬁ-
ciency remains a signiﬁcant challenge in urban trafﬁc object
detection [14, 15].
Methodologies
We propose RTL-Net, a novel architecture that incorporates
three key innovations: an improved evaluation mechanism
called PIoU, a lightweight detection head design LSCD,
and an enhanced feature extraction module DWR. Addi-
tionally, we improve the feature fusion network by adopting
the BiFPN design concept. These modiﬁcations result in an
enhanced algorithm that maintains lightweight performance
while signiﬁcantly improving the detection capabilities for
remote sensing images. Figure1 illustrates the architecture
of our proposed RTL-Net.
Powerful-IoU
In various deep learning models, intersection over union
(IoU) is a crucial metric for evaluating model performance in
tasks such as object detection and segmentation. However,
traditional IoU metrics demonstrate signiﬁcant limitations
in handling overlapping regions [25], particularly in sce-
narios with high degrees of overlap or fuzzy boundaries,
which can result in inaccurate performance evaluations [26,
27]. To address these limitations in complex scenarios,
Powerable-IoU (P-IoU) [28, 29] enhances the traditional IoU
by incorporating the ratio between intersection and union
and a more comprehensive evaluation factor for object size,
shape, and position. To improve the robustness and accuracy
of object detection evaluation, we introduce target adaptive
penalty.

Dilation-wise residual
Residual connections have been proven to be an effective
network structure in traditional deep learning and convolu-
tional neural networks, which facilitate the learning of more
complex features and address issues such as vanishing and
exploding gradients by directly adding the input signal to the
output of the subsequent layer, thereby enhancing network
training and performance. Dilatation-wise Residual (DWR)
[31] is an extension of the residual network, which is primar-
ily optimized to enhance the receptive ﬁeld in convolution
operations. The Dilation operation inserts holes in the con-
volution kernel, increasing the size of the receptive ﬁeld and
allowing a broader range of context information to be cap-
tured.

Bidirectional feature pyramid network
Feature Pyramid Networks (FPN) and Path Aggregation
Networks (PAN) are frequently used in traditional feature
fusion networks due to their effective ability to combine hier-
archical feature information. Figure6 illustrates the structure
of this model.
FPN implements a top-down propagation path, where
small-size feature maps undergo upsampling and fusion
with horizontally connected feature maps of the same size,
followed by 3×3 convolution operations. This operation
is repeated in stages to transfer the deep, semantic solid
information to the shallow layer. PAN complements this
with a bottom-up propagation path, applying down-sampling
operations to large-size feature maps before fusion with
laterally connected features of matching dimensions. The
same process is followed stage by stage for the next layer
size to enhance the ability of the network to extract fusion
features by transferring the robust positioning information
to the deeper layer. However, traditional implementations
often employ uniform weights or simple addition for fea-
ture fusion, leading to potential information loss at certain
scales. This particularly affects the detection of small objects
or those in complex backgrounds in remote sensing images.
To address these limitations, we incorporate the Bidi-
rectional Feature Pyramid Networks (BiFPN) [32] design.
Figure7 illustrates the principle of its improved structure.
First, the backbone network extracts the feature maps at
different scales. Multiple feature layers are fused using bidi-

In remote sensing images, BiFPN aims to improve object
detection through the use of multiscale features. Fusing the
information from multi-level feature maps provides a more
ﬂexible and efﬁcient way of feature transfer. BiFPN is char-
acterized by its bidirectional connection mechanism, which
allows information to ﬂow from low-level features to high-
level features in a bidirectional manner. Unlike traditional
feature pyramid networks, which fuse features from top
to bottom, BiFPN uses reverse connections during feature
fusion, thus enhancing complementary information between
features. Additionally, BiFPN employs a learnable weight-
ing mechanism that automatically assigns different fusion
weights based on feature importance [33, 34]. This enables
the network to select more representative components from
features at different scales, thereby improving the overall
feature representation capability. This efﬁcient structure not
only accelerates model training but also reduces computa-
tional resource consumption [35]. This approach repeatedly
applies top-down and bottom-up bidirectional feature fusion,
leading to improved accuracy and efﬁciency in object detec-
tion tasks.

Ablation study
We conducted ablation experiments under identical condi-
tions to evaluate the effectiveness of each improved module
and its contribution to the overall model performance.
YOLOv8s algorithm on MS COCO dataset is shown in
Table 2 as a function of different loss functions.
Compared with classical object detection networks, RTL-
Net achieves a Mean Average Precision (mAP) of 42.3%,
representing a signiﬁcant improvement of 2.3% over pre-
vious approaches. This performance surpasses all related
models, demonstrating its comprehensive superiority.
For small target detection, particularly pedestrians, bicy-
cles, and tricycles, RTL-Net outperforms both YOLOv8s
and the recent YOLOv10s model. These results demonstrate
that our designed DWR module signiﬁcantly improves small
object detection capabilities.
For Car, Van, Truck and Motor detection, RTL-Net
achieves excellent results of 76.6%, 52.4%, 53.5% and
41.0% respectively, ranking among the top performers.
These results demonstrate both the algorithm’s superiority in
these critical categories and its balanced performance across
various object classes.
Based on the experimental data in Table 2, the PIoU loss
function demonstrates advantages in detection accuracy and
target localization compared to mainstream loss functions
like CIoU, GIoU, and Focal-EIoU. Its improved measure-
ment of box overlap enables better parameter optimization
during training. It also proves the importance of selecting an
appropriate loss function to improve the performance of the
object detection task.
Table 3 evaluates the impact of different modules and
their combinations on both detection and lightweight per-
formance of YOLOv8s. Results show that all proposed
modules—PIoU, LSCD, DWR and BiFPN—positively con-
tribute to the algorithm’s detection accuracy. As a result of
the improvements in detection accuracy of LSCD, DWR,
and BiFPN, the algorithm also performs well in lightweight
performance, demonstrating that these modules effectively
reduce the complexity and computational overhead of the
model while maintaining performance. It is noteworthy that
BiFPN achieved the best results on all indicators, demon-
strating the efﬁciency of our feature pyramid optimization.
Its weighted fusion mechanism can help the model ﬁnd a
good balance between the degree of lightweight and accu-
racy to achieve better performance.
While the DWR module and LSCD show moderate
improvements in overall metrics, they signiﬁcantly enhance
small object detection accuracy, which is crucial for prac-
tical applications. In addition, the PIoU module performs
exceptionally well in improving the detection frame rate,
showing strong generalization ability, which provides strong
support for efﬁcient and accurate object detection. These
results verify each module’s effectiveness and provide an
essential reference for future research.

improving the detection performance of dense small targets.
Conclusion
We propose RTL-Net, an improved lightweight network
based on YOLOv8s, to address the challenges of deep
learning-basedremotesensingimageobjectdetection.Rebuild-
ing the baseline model, implementing lightweight improve-
ment modules, and optimizing the feature fusion network
resulted in an overall 2.3% improvement in detection accu-

racy, and a 263.2 FPS. A comparison and analysis of
experimental data and visualizations shows that the improved
algorithm can detect small and occluded objects accurately in
real-time and meet remote sensing image detection require-
ments. Furthermore, the model size is reduced by 9.4 MB
and the number of parameters and computations is reduced
by 43.9% and 18.9%, respectively. In intelligent transporta-
tion and autonomous driving, the algorithm has a wide range
of practical applications that are essential to the construction
of smart cities. The performance of the proposed algorithm
could be more robust for more complex scenes, especially
in people detection, and does not surpass the YOLOX-s and
YOLOv7 algorithms.
The key research topics in the future will focus on
improving the ability of dense crowd detection [39–42] and
robustness in multiple complex scenes, or we can validate
the superiority of RTL-Net through comprehensive testing
on embedded devices to investigate hardware-aware neu-
ral architecture search for efﬁcient deployment [43, 44]and
develop dynamic inference schemes [45, 46] to further bal-
ance accuracy and latency constraints.

Abstract: Object detection algorithm in urban trafﬁc using remote sensing images often suffers from high complexity, low real-time performance, and low accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose RTL-Net, an urban trafﬁc object detection network structure based on You Only Look Once (YOLO) v8s. To enhance real-time performance beyond the benchmark, we imple- mented lightweight designs for the loss function, backbone, neck, and head components. Firstly, a Powerable-IoU (PIoU) loss function was introduced to make the algorithm more suitable for different scales of targets and reduce false detection. Sec- ondly, the Lightweight Shared Convolutional Detection (LSCD) head was replaced to ensure the detection performance and signiﬁcantly improve the lightweight performance of the algorithm. Additionally, this paper introduces the Dilatation-wise Residual (DWR) module to facilitate the algorithm’s extraction of detailed features. In addition, we optimize the Bidirec- tional Feature Pyramid Network (Bi-FPN), enabling the fusion of multiple features to improve overall feature integration and performance. The VisDrone2021 dataset was utilized for experimental training. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves a signiﬁcant 43.9% reduction in parameters and an 18.9% decrease in computational complexity. Moreover, the detection accuracy has improved by 2.3%, while maintaining a real-time detection speed of 263.2 frames per second. For edge computing object detection, our method outperforms YOLOv8s and leading remote sensing algorithms in both speed and accuracy, achieving state-of-the-art performance among single-stage detectors with comparable parameters.
